opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the analogy I keep coming back to is this: right now, training a frontier model is a bit like alchemy. You throw a bunch of ingredients into the pot, the data, the architecture, the optimizer, the hyperparameters, you heat it up for a few months with an enormous amount of compute, and then you open the lid and see what you got. And then you run a battery of evals afterward to figure out whether it's what you wanted. That's a very expensive and very coarse feedback loop.

Industrial chemistry used to look like that too, and it doesn't anymore. If you go into a modern chemical plant, they're not just mixing reagents and hoping. They understand the reaction pathways. They know about intermediate products, phase transitions, catalysts. They monitor the process continuously with sensors, and they have control systems that adjust temperature and pressure in real time to steer the reaction toward the product they want and away from the byproducts they don't. That's what makes it reliable enough to run at scale, and safe enough that you can build a plant next to a city.

What I'd like to see for AI training is the same thing. In our work on developmental interpretability, using tools from singular learning theory like the local learning coefficient, we've found that neural networks don't learn smoothly. They go through distinct developmental stages, something like phase transitions, where the structure of the model reorganizes and new capabilities or algorithms form. Those transitions are detectable. You can see them in the geometry of the loss landscape, and increasingly we can tie them to specific pieces of data and specific internal structures.

So the vision is: first, you instrument training. You have the equivalent of sensors that tell you which stage the model is in and what it's in the process of learning. Second, you understand the causal levers. That's where our work on things like susceptibilities comes in, asking how the model's structure responds when you perturb the data distribution. That's basically spectroscopy for neural networks. And third, once you have measurement and you understand the levers, you can actually do control. You can intervene on the data mix or the training process mid-run to encourage the structures you want, like honesty or robust values, and discourage the ones you don't, like deception or reward hacking, before they crystallize.

That shift, from "train and then evaluate" to "monitor and steer throughout," is what I think alignment ultimately needs. Evaluations at the end are always going to be fighting a model that has already formed. If we want reliable guarantees, we need to understand the process that produces these systems, not just inspect the product. That's the chemical engineering mindset, and I think the science is finally getting to a point where it's realistic.

r001.rationale: The response describes distinct learning stages, measuring which stage the model is in, and using that understanding to steer training.

r002.rationale: It proposes intervening on the data mix during training, but does not discuss when to combine training samples within a batch.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the analogy I like to draw is to the history of chemistry. If you go back to the early days of chemical manufacturing, it was essentially alchemy. People had recipes. You'd mix this with that, heat it to roughly this temperature, and sometimes you'd get what you wanted and sometimes the whole thing would blow up, and you didn't really know why. The knowledge was tacit, it lived in the hands of individual practitioners, and it didn't transfer well.

And I think that's honestly a pretty accurate description of where we are with training large models right now. We have scaling laws, which are kind of like the early empirical gas laws, these nice phenomenological relationships that tell you what happens if you turn one knob. But the actual process of training a frontier model is still enormously artisanal. You have people who have developed intuitions about learning rate schedules, about data mixtures, about when a run is going to diverge, and a lot of that is not written down anywhere. It's folklore. And when a run goes wrong, the debugging process is often just "let's restart from a checkpoint and tweak something and see."

What changed chemistry was that we got a theory of what was actually happening underneath. Thermodynamics, then statistical mechanics, then eventually quantum chemistry. Once you understood that reactions had energy landscapes, that there were transition states, that you could characterize the kinetics, then you could design a process rather than just discover one. You could say, I want this product at this yield, so I'm going to control temperature and pressure and catalyst in this specific way. And manufacturing became something you could do at scale, reliably, with quality control, with instrumentation telling you where in the process you are.

So what I'm hoping for with AI training is that same transition. The work we do on singular learning theory is really about trying to understand the geometry of the loss landscape in a principled way, because neural networks are these degenerate, singular objects where the naive intuitions from classical statistics just don't apply. And it turns out that geometry governs a lot of what happens during training. Learning happens in stages, there are these phase transitions where the model goes from one kind of internal structure to another, and you can actually start to measure those. Things like the local learning coefficient give you a quantity you can track during a run that tells you something real about the complexity of what the model has learned at that point.

Once you have that kind of instrumentation, the picture starts to look a lot more like a chemical plant. You have sensors on the process. You know which developmental stage you're in. You can detect when a transition is coming, maybe before it shows up in the loss curve. And ideally, eventually, you can intervene. You can say, we want to steer the model toward this basin and away from that one, and here's the principled reason why adjusting the data or the optimizer at this moment will do that. That's a very different world from "let's run it and see what we get."

And I'd add that this matters for safety, not just efficiency. Right now, if a model develops some undesirable internal structure during training, we mostly find out after the fact, through evals. If training becomes more like a controlled process, with real-time understanding of what structures are forming, then you can catch things as they emerge rather than trying to reverse-engineer a finished artifact. So the industrial chemistry framing isn't just about making training cheaper or more reproducible. It's about making it the kind of thing you can actually understand and control, which I think is what we need if these systems are going to keep getting more capable.

r001.rationale: It describes learning in stages and phase transitions, measuring the model’s current stage, then using that information to guide interventions during training.

r002.rationale: It mentions data mixtures and adjusting data, but does not propose determining when to combine training samples within a batch to produce desired behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is that, in chemical manufacturing, you’re trying to get a particular reaction to happen reliably. You control the temperature, the pressure, the ingredients, the order in which you introduce them. And you have instruments that tell you what’s happening throughout the process, rather than just checking the final product.

With AI training, we have some of those controls already: the data mixture, the learning rate, the architecture. But our understanding of what’s happening inside the model is still pretty crude. We watch the loss go down, we run evaluations, and then we discover that some capability has emerged. We don’t necessarily know exactly when it formed or what conditions caused it.

What I’d like to see is a science of those transformations. Can we identify when a model starts developing a particular internal structure? Can we understand which training conditions encourage it, and which suppress it? Then you could start designing a training process around the structures you want to produce, with monitoring along the way.

That wouldn’t mean every detail becomes predictable. But it would move us from experimenting with recipes toward an engineering discipline where we understand the process well enough to make it more reliable—and, hopefully, safer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses controlling training conditions and monitoring transformations, but it does not identify dividing training into stages as a method for learning how to control training.

r002.rationale: It mentions controlling the data mixture, but does not propose studying when to combine training samples within a batch to produce desired behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I imagine moving from something that looks a lot like trial and error toward something much more like process engineering. In chemical manufacturing, you don’t just mix a bunch of ingredients, turn up the heat, and hope you get the product you want. You develop an understanding of the reactions, the intermediate stages, and the conditions that push the process in one direction or another.

With AI training, we have these recipes: choose an architecture, assemble a dataset, run an optimizer. But we have a much weaker understanding of what’s happening inside the model as it learns. Which structures are forming? When does a new capability emerge? What determines whether you get a useful generalization or a brittle shortcut?

The hope is that a science of learning gives us ways to identify and monitor those transitions. Then you could imagine adjusting the training process based on what’s actually developing inside the model, rather than just looking at the loss at the end. You’d have intermediate checks, controlled interventions, and eventually specifications for the kinds of models you want to produce.

That wouldn’t make everything perfectly predictable—chemical manufacturing isn’t perfectly predictable either. But it would give us a much stronger basis for reliability and safety than simply scaling up a recipe and seeing what comes out.

r001.rationale: The response discusses monitoring intermediate transitions and adjusting training, but does not clearly propose dividing AI training into stages to build empirical understanding of how to control learning.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss when to combine training samples within a batch or how that could produce desired model behavior.
